client: Lately I've been feeling like I'm drowning in grad school work, but I can't afford to quit my job at the coffee shop. Every time I try to focus on my thesis, I keep thinking about my next shift, and when I'm at work, I'm stressing about falling behind in my classes. Honestly, I'm not sure how talking about this will help when what I really need is more hours in the day.
therapist:
I hear how overwhelming this balancing act feels for you—like no matter where you put your energy, the other responsibility pulls at you. That sense of being stretched thin can make it hard to see a way forward.  

What happens when you notice those thoughts about work during study time, or school worries during your shift? Do they feel like facts, or more like a mental alarm going off?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: They feel like... both? Like obviously it's true I have shifts and deadlines, but my brain makes it feel way more catastrophic than it probably is. Like if I'm reading a research paper, suddenly I'll get this panicky thought like "You're going to get fired if you don't check the work schedule RIGHT NOW" even though I know my boss wouldn't fire me over that. It's exhausting.
therapist:
It sounds like your thoughts are amplifying the stakes, even when you know logically that things aren't as dire as they feel in the moment. That disconnect between what you know and what you feel can be so draining.  

When those catastrophic thoughts pop up, what do you usually do to help ground yourself? Or does it feel like they just take over completely?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Most of the time they just take over. I'll try to take deep breaths sometimes, but then I start thinking "You're wasting time breathing when you should be working!" and that makes it worse. It's like I can't win - either I panic or I feel guilty for trying not to panic.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught in a really tough cycle—where even your attempts to cope get twisted into more pressure. That "can't win" feeling makes so much sense when every option seems to backfire.  

I'm curious, when those thoughts accuse you of "wasting time," do they sound like your own voice, or more like someone else's expectations you've internalized?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That's... actually really uncomfortable to think about. It does sound like my dad's voice sometimes. He was always on me about "idle hands" growing up, even when I was a kid doing normal kid stuff. But now it's like I don't need him to say it anymore because my brain does it for him. Isn't that messed up?
therapist:
It makes complete sense that this realization would feel uncomfortable—that critical voice from childhood has become so ingrained it feels automatic now. That’s a really painful pattern to notice.  

What’s it like to recognize that this isn’t just *your* voice, but one you inherited? Does that change how you see those "wasting time" thoughts at all?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: It's weird... when you put it that way, the thoughts feel less true somehow? Like if it's just my dad's old baggage, maybe I don't have to believe them so much. But then I immediately feel guilty for thinking that, like I'm blaming him when I'm the one who can't get my act together.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between two painful places—questioning those old messages but then feeling disloyal for doing so. That guilt seems to add another layer of weight when you're already carrying so much.  

What do you imagine might happen if you allowed yourself to set down just a little bit of that inherited pressure? Even for an hour?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, the idea of letting go of that pressure for even an hour makes me nervous. Like if I relax for a minute, everything will collapse. But at the same time... I'm so tired. Maybe I could try it during my lunch break tomorrow? Though knowing me, I'll probably just sit there stressing about not stressing.
therapist:
That nervousness about "everything collapsing" if you relax shows how deeply you've come to believe that constant pressure is what keeps you afloat—even though it's exhausting you.  

The fact that you're considering trying this during lunch, even with hesitation, feels like an important step. What would make that experiment feel slightly safer to try? Maybe setting a timer or choosing a specific spot?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Setting a timer might help... but I think I'd still spend the whole time watching it count down. The idea of choosing a spot is interesting though. There's this bench under a tree near campus that's usually quiet. Maybe if I went there with a book that has nothing to do with school? But then I'd probably just feel guilty about bringing leisure reading instead of my thesis articles.
therapist:
It sounds like even as you consider this small act of kindness to yourself, part of you is already anticipating how the guilt might creep in. That bench under the tree sounds lovely—what is it about that particular spot that makes it feel different from other places?  

When you imagine bringing a leisure book there, what emotion comes up first—just before the guilt arrives?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: The bench is... peaceful in a way nowhere else is lately. No students rushing to class or coworkers needing things. Just for a second, when I imagine sitting there, I feel this tiny spark of relief. But it's immediately followed by panic—like I'm being irresponsible for wanting that peace.
therapist: It sounds like that bench offers a rare moment of calm, but the conflict between wanting that peace and feeling like it's "irresponsible" is so palpable. That tiny spark of relief you described feels important—what would it be like to hold onto that spark, even just for a few seconds longer, before the panic rushes in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Holding onto that spark feels... scary, honestly. Like if I let myself feel even a little bit of relief, I'll lose my edge or something. But at the same time, I'm so tired of feeling this wound up all the time. I guess I could try focusing on that spark for just a few breaths tomorrow at the bench, but I'm not sure I'll be able to stop the panic from taking over.
therapist:
It makes sense that holding onto that spark feels scary—like it might unravel the tight control you've worked so hard to maintain. That tension between wanting relief and fearing it is so real.  

Taking just a few breaths with that spark tomorrow could be a gentle experiment—not to stop the panic, but to notice how both the relief and the panic can exist together. How does that idea sit with you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually makes me feel a little less trapped, like I don't have to completely defeat the panic to have moments of peace. But part of me still thinks this is just avoiding the "real work" - shouldn't I be trying to eliminate these anxious thoughts completely instead of just coexisting with them?
therapist:
It sounds like there's a part of you that believes peace can only come when you've fully "fixed" or eliminated these anxious thoughts—like coexisting with them isn't enough. That's a really common belief, especially when we're used to being hard on ourselves.  

What would it mean to you if coexisting with these thoughts *was* part of the "real work," rather than avoiding it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
